tagline: Reorganize debts and protect property with Chapter 13 in Iowa.

blocks.html:
Filing for Chapter 13 bankruptcy allows Iowa residents with steady incomes to reorganize debt while protecting important personal assets. Rather than liquidating property, this process consolidates obligations into a manageable three- to five-year court-approved repayment plan.

This guide explains how Chapter 13 bankruptcy works in Iowa, who qualifies, and how it impacts your financial future.

What Is Chapter 13 Bankruptcy in Iowa and How Does It Work?

Chapter 13 bankruptcy is a legal process for people with a regular income who are struggling with debt. Instead of wiping out debts right away, this process lets you create a plan to pay back some or all of what you owe over three to five years.

When you file for Chapter 13, the court puts an “automatic stay” in place. This temporary order generally stops most creditors from trying to collect money from you. It may prevent them from taking money from your paycheck, suing you, or taking your property. Moreover, the automatic stay typically stops most collection actions, including phone calls, lawsuits, wage garnishments, and foreclosure proceedings, as long as your case remains active and in compliance.

While this protection is active, you will typically make one monthly payment to a person called a Chapter 13 trustee, who then distributes that money to your creditors based on your repayment plan.

Chapter 13 is different from Chapter 7 bankruptcy. Before your plan is finalized, it has to be approved by the bankruptcy court, which will review your income, expenses, and debts to ensure the plan is fair.

This generally erases any remaining unsecured debts, like credit card bills or medical expenses.

Eligibility for Chapter 13

Chapter 13 is generally available to individuals and sole proprietors with a regular, steady income. To qualify, you typically need to meet the following requirements:

  • Your total secured and unsecured debt does not exceed $2,750,000.
  • You did not withdraw a prior bankruptcy petition within the last 180 days because creditors sought relief.
  • The bankruptcy court did not dismiss any bankruptcy petition within 180 days due to your failure to appear or comply with court orders.
  • You obtained a credit counseling certificate within 180 days before your initial filing.
  • Your disposable income, your monthly income minus necessary living expenses, is enough to cover the monthly payment amount throughout the repayment period.

Chapter 13 debt limits are adjusted periodically. For cases filed on or after April 1, 2025, the eligibility limits are generally $526,700 in unsecured debts and $1,580,125 in secured debts.

These amounts are set to remain in effect through March 31, 2028, when the next statutory three-year adjustment takes place.

What Debts Can You Discharge in Chapter 13 Bankruptcy?

In Chapter 13, debts are sorted into categories, which affects how they are paid and whether they may be discharged once the plan is complete.

Priority Unsecured Debts

Priority debts are among the most important obligations under bankruptcy law, and your repayment plan will typically need to pay them in full. Common examples include:

  • Recent income taxes
  • Child support or alimony
  • Certain government fines
  • Unpaid wages you owe if you own a business

Generally, these debts are addressed before other types of debt are handled under your plan.

Secured Debts

Secured debts are loans that are tied to a specific piece of property, known as collateral. If you stop making payments, the creditor can typically take back the property. The most common examples are:

  • Home mortgages
  • Car loans
  • Other loans secured by property, like equipment

In Chapter 13, your plan generally has to pay at least the value of the property securing the debt. It may also allow you to catch up on missed payments for your house or car over the plan’s duration, helping you keep your property.

General Unsecured Debts

General unsecured debts are not backed by any property and are not considered priority debts. These often include:

  • Credit card debt
  • Medical bills
  • Personal loans
  • Past-due utility bills

In a Chapter 13 plan, these creditors generally have to receive at least what they would have if you had filed for Chapter 7 instead. After you make all your payments under the plan, any remaining balance on these types of debts is typically discharged.

How Chapter 13 Bankruptcy Manages Non-Dischargeable Debts

Some debts, however, may not be erased in Chapter 13. These generally include most student loans, child support, alimony, and certain fines from criminal cases.

Nevertheless, Chapter 13 allows you to reorganize these obligations through a structured repayment plan, providing significant relief even when full elimination isn’t available.

For child support and alimony, which are classified as priority debts, Chapter 13 generally requires that they be paid in full over the repayment period. This structure may prevent the accumulation of arrears by ensuring consistent payments are made toward these obligations.

Student loans, while generally non-dischargeable, can typically be included in your Chapter 13 repayment plan. Although the debt may remain at the end of the plan, incorporating it into a repayment schedule can help you stay current and potentially avoid penalties or collection activity.

Chapter 13 Bankruptcy Filing Process in Iowa

If you meet the requirements for filing bankruptcy under Chapter 13 and are ready to move forward, here’s a step-by-step guide to the filing process:

Step 1: Consult a Bankruptcy Lawyer

Starting with a bankruptcy attorney is typically an important first step. Chapter 13 involves several stages and a significant amount of paperwork, so working with someone well-versed in the process can make a real difference.

Step 2: Credit Counseling Course

Before you can file for debt relief, you’ll typically need to complete a credit counseling course from a court-approved agency; this is a requirement under federal law. In it, you’ll review your finances and learn about other options available to you.

Once you finish, you’ll receive a certificate that you’ll need to include with your filing paperwork, and it generally has to be less than 180 days old.

Step 3: File the Bankruptcy Petition

To move forward, you’ll complete a bankruptcy petition and file it with the bankruptcy court that serves your county. You’ll typically also need to file financial documents, including:

  • Schedules of assets and liabilities
  • The schedule of current income
  • The schedule of executory contracts and unexpired leases
  • Tax returns and transcripts

After filing, you’ll generally be assigned a trustee who will distribute your monthly payments to creditors and oversee your case throughout the repayment period.

Step 4: Develop a Repayment Plan

Within 14 days of filing, you will generally need to create a Chapter 13 repayment plan, your proposal for paying back your debts over three to five years. The length of the plan typically depends on how much you earn. The court will then hold a hearing to review your plan, checking whether it complies with applicable legal rules for repaying different types of debt, such as mortgages, car loans, and credit card bills.

Step 5: Monthly Payments

You start making the agreed monthly payments to the trustee within a month of filing, even if the court has not yet approved the plan. After the plan confirmation hearing, the trustee will typically distribute payments to your creditors in order of priority.

Step 6: Receive a Discharge

After completing your repayment period and the debtor education course, you may be entitled to a discharge. The court will generally assess whether you paid all priority debts, and if you qualify, remaining unsecured debts may be discharged.

items.q: What debts can be included in a Chapter 13 bankruptcy?
items.a: Chapter 13 may include many types of debts, such as credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, past-due mortgage payments, car loans, certain tax debts, and arrears on secured obligations. Some debts, like most student loans and recent child support or alimony, are generally not dischargeable but can typically be managed through your repayment plan.

items.q: Will I lose my home or car if I file Chapter 13 bankruptcy?
items.a: Chapter 13 typically allows you to catch up on missed payments over time while continuing to make current payments, as long as you follow the court-approved repayment plan.

items.q: What happens if I miss a Chapter 13 payment?
items.a: Missing payments may put your case at risk. Depending on the situation, the trustee or creditors may request dismissal or other consequences. In some cases, a plan modification may be possible, but continued nonpayment generally results in the loss of debt relief protection.
